• Name: Marron crayfish
  • Scientific name: Cherax tenuimanus / Cherax cainii
  • Other names: Hairy Marron / Smooth marron
  • Minimum tank size: 500 litres (130 gallons)
  • Keeping: Easy
  • Breeding: Easy-Medium
  • Size: up to 38 cm (15 inches)
  • Temperature: 20–24°C (68–75°F)
  • pH: 7.0–9.0
  • GH: 8–20
  • Diet: Omnivore
  • Temperament: Aggressive
  • Lifespan: up to 10 years
  • Colour: Brown

Cherax tenuimanus (Hairy marron or Margaret River marron) is endemic to the Margaret River in southwestern Australia. It is naturally restricted: it is known from only eleven sites along a section of the river, in an area less than 50 km in length.

Cherax cainii (Smooth marron) occurs over much of the south-west of Western Australia (as far east as Esperance and as far north as Geraldton), where it supports a popular recreational fishery and aquaculture industry. More recently it was introduced into South Africa, Zimbabwe, Japan, the USA, China and the Caribbean as a commercial aquaculture species.

These crayfish prefer clear, fast-flowing streams and rivers with sandy bottoms and abundant vegetation. The water is soft, acidic and high in tannins. Cool, flowing, well-oxygenated water allows them to thrive, while they tend to avoid stagnant backwaters. Ideal habitat consists of freshwater with plentiful vegetation, woody debris, rocky banks and muddy substrates.

The minimum recommended tank size for one Marron crayfish is 500 litres (130 gallons). A pair (male and female) needs at least 120 litres (40 gallons). Larger tanks are preferable for stable water chemistry and easier creation of hiding areas.

  • Too many crayfish in insufficient space leads to aggression, injuries and cannibalism. Overcrowding is the main source of stress, particularly with more than one male.
  • Long tanks are better than tall tanks of the same size, as crayfish need to crawl from side to side rather than up and down.
  • Crayfish are good escape artists. Cover the tank with a stable lid, as they are strong enough to move it.

Temperature: 20–24°C (68–75°F). They tolerate low temperatures but stop growing below 12.5°C (55°F). Growth also declines rapidly above 24°C (75°F), with mortality at 30°C (86°F) and above.

pH: 7.0–9.0.

Hardness: GH 8–20 (hard water).

Oxygen: dissolved oxygen should be kept at or above 6 mg/L. They become stressed below 3 mg/L. They need good aeration and water flow.

Salinity: they may tolerate salinities of 0 to 15 ppt, although not necessarily reproduce in them. Growth decreases above 6–8 ppt.

Filters: no special requirements; any filter suited to the tank size will do. Sponge filters can be a bad idea, as the crayfish chip and chew on them and will eventually shred them.

Lighting: no special requirements. They are nocturnal and used to very little light. If you have plants or other animals, adapt the lighting to their needs.

Substrate: no special requirements; these crayfish are not diggers.

Decorations: decorations mainly provide shelter, so the more the better. They appreciate all types of leaves, rocks, driftwood, PVC pipes, etc.

These crayfish are omnivorous scavengers, feeding on both plant and animal matter, including aquatic plants, decaying vegetation, dead organic matter, algae, small insects, insect larvae, worms, snails, crustaceans, tadpoles, frogs and fish eggs/fry. They are opportunistic feeders and adjust their diet to food availability.

For optimal growth they require a diet of 30–40% protein at 10–15% of body weight per week (about 2% of body weight per day if fed daily). As this is hard to calculate, it is enough if the food does not exceed the size of the carapace.

Suggested foods in aquariums: leaves, plants, blanched vegetables, crushed snails, earthworms, dead fish or shrimp, bloodworms, detritus worms, tubifex worms, blackworms.

  • Feeding frequency: 3–4 times a week for adults; daily for juveniles.
  • Feed before lights out.
  • Leave food for 24 hours before removing it; remove leftovers by siphoning before adding fresh food. Leaves can stay for several days.
  • Leave old exoskeletons in the tank.
  • Check hiding places from time to time, as they store food there, to prevent bacterial contamination.
  • Vary the diet periodically.

Marron crayfish are crepuscular or nocturnal, most active just after sunset. During the day they stay hidden under logs, rocks and debris. They are solitary and generally do not share hiding spots.

They can be aggressive toward each other and other crayfish, especially when defending territory, competing for food or mating. Males in particular fight with their large claws. When threatened they move rapidly backward by curling and unfolding the abdomen. They are non-burrowing and prefer to live under shelter.

They are not compatible with live plants: they eat, cut, shred and uproot everything. Viable options are plastic plants, floating plants or cheap plants you are ready to lose.

Keeping them with other crayfish or even conspecifics is not recommended, as they grow very big and will eventually fight. They can also be hostile to fish, crabs, dwarf frogs and especially freshwater snails. Bottom-dwelling, slow-moving or long-finned fish (like Betta) are the first to get hurt.

  • Social: No
  • Active: No
  • Peaceful: No
  • Territorial: Yes
  • Burrowers: No

Cherax cainii grows slightly faster than Cherax tenuimanus and is more readily bred, including in captivity. The two species can successfully hybridize.

Maturity: at least 2 to 3 years, at a total body length of 8–11 cm (3.1–4.3 inches).

Mating: the eggs take nearly half a year to develop inside the females. The male deposits a spermatophore between the female's 5th pair of legs.

Eggs: females incubate on average 200–400 eggs for 12–16 weeks on the pleopods under the tail (large females may produce up to 800), from which about 150–250 juveniles are released.

Hatching: newly hatched young cannot live separately from the mother for a further 2–4 weeks. They need to molt before becoming completely independent. Females whose young have become independent should be separated from females still carrying eggs or young to prevent cannibalism.

Molting: exoskeletons do not grow, so crayfish molt as they grow. Calcium is essential for the new exoskeleton, and molting leaves them vulnerable. Before molting they become less active, stop eating and seek shelter; otherwise they easily fall prey to tankmates.

Two types of crayfish share the name "Marron crayfish". Despite being closely related and similar, to the extent of potential hybridization, Cherax cainii has proven more successful and better adapted. Cherax tenuimanus is listed as rare under the Western Australian Wildlife Conservation Act 1950 and managed as 'critically endangered' (IUCN criteria) by the Western Australian Government (CALM 2005).

Taxonomy: Cherax tenuimanus was first described by G.W. Smith in 1912. In the 1980s a closely related crayfish was discovered in the same region and, based on electrophoretic and morphological differences, marron were split into two subspecies. In 2002 the new subspecies was elevated to species based on allozyme data and named Cherax cainii.

Etymology: Cherax is thought to derive from the Greek "Kherax", meaning "a kind of lobster" or "crayfish", or possibly from "charax", a pointed stake, referring to the sharp rostrum and spiny claws. "Tenuimanus" combines Latin "tenuis" (thin, slender) and "manus" (hand, limb), referring to the slender claws.

Description: one of the largest crayfish in the world, growing to more than 38 cm (15 inches) and recorded over 2 kg (4.4 lb). Smooth marron can reach 60–150 g in 12 months and 100–300 g in 24 months. Hairy marron have a median carina extending continuously to the cervical groove, prominent tufts of long recumbent setae, and no tuberculation on the areola compared to Smooth marron. Marron have spines on the telson. They are generally dark brown, good camouflage in tannin-rich southern waters; an electric blue variety is raised for aquariums and an orange-striped marron was recently found in the south-west. Lifespan can exceed 10 years in optimal tank conditions.
